The apparent matter is that their condition today, and indeed tomorrow, is like their condition yesterday. The Words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾. The conjoined element is a predicate (khabar) like the element it is conjoined to. By "the star" (al-najm) is meant the plant that comes up (yanjumu), that is, appears and rises from the earth, having no stem; and by "the tree" (al-shajar) is meant the plant that has a stem. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr and Abu Razin. By their prostration is meant their submission to Him, the Exalted, in what He wills for them by nature. Their running according to the requirements of their natures is likened to the submission of one who prostrates to his Creator and his exalting Him. Then the name of the thing likened to (al-mushabbah bihi) is used for the thing likened (al-mushabbah), so there is a clear, subordinate metaphor (istiʿarah tasrihiyyah tabaʿiyyah).

Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan said that "the star" is the star of the sky, its prostration being its setting and the like, and the prostration of the tree being its shadow and its turning; this is the view of Mujahid and al-Hasan. In another report from Mujahid, their prostration is an expression for their submission to what He, Glorified is He, wills for them by nature. The majority hold the tafsir of "the star" to be what you heard first, because its being joined with "the tree" indicates it, although the prior mention of "the sun and the moon" may give the impression that it has its well-known meaning, and so there is a clear double meaning (tawriyah zahirah).

The omission of the conjunction (al-ʿatif) from the second, third and fourth clauses, because they come in the manner of enumeration, indicates that each of what they contain is a独立 blessing requiring thanks, and they (people) have fallen short in rendering it. Had they been conjoined, despite their close connection and harmony, it might have been supposed that all of them were one blessing.

The placement of the conjunction between the fourth and the fifth is for the sake of their harmony in terms of contrast: "the sun and the moon" are heavenly, and "the star and the tree" are earthly; and in that each of the state of the heavenly and the state of the earthly is of the category of submission to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and in that they are free of a verbal link while being two predicates, relying on the perfect strength of the semantic connection, since it cannot be supposed that the mind would go to the sun and moon's state being subject to other than Him, nor to the star's and tree's prostration being to anyone other than Him, Glorified is He. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon run by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." Thus they have said.

In al-Kashf, clarifying what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned in this context: he omitted the conjunction from the clauses before "The sun and the moon by a reckoning", because the purpose is enumerating blessings and rebuking the one who denies them, as one says: "Zayd has made you rich after poverty, honored you after humiliation, multiplied you after scarcity, and done to you what no one has done to anyone." Whatever of his kindness is denied, it is as if, having enumerated one blessing, he stirs the listener so that he reflects whether he has given thanks for it as it deserves or not, then moves on to another. Had the conjunction been brought, they would have become like one unit and there would have been no stirring at all. When the need for the stirring enumeration and rebuke was fulfilled by mentioning what is the root of the blessings, in the manner of returning the speech to its original course of enumerating blessings one after another, in harmony and proximity, with the conjunctive particle, and in this is an alert that blessings cannot be counted, so let one suffice with enumerating their most exalted in rank for the stated purpose.

The clause "The sun and the moon by a reckoning" is not among the predicates of the subject. Al-Zamakhshari only asked about the reason for the connection, and answered that the connection is achieved by semantic conjunction: as if, after he had rebuked and alerted, he began to enumerate the roots of the blessings so as to establish what He asked of him in thanks. This is like what you say in the previous example, after your words "he did to you what no one has done to anyone": "his peers submitted to him, his brothers obeyed him, he extended his bounty to those under his dominion, and no one was excluded from the shelter of his justice and fairness." No one with understanding doubts that these are clauses detached from the first in grammatical construction, yet connected to it by a semantic connection, which the detachment of its purpose produced, since these were brought for one aim and those for another. Near to this connection is the connection of His, Exalted is He, words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], the verse, with His words: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], the verse. End of quotation. In my view the intended meaning has been pushed too far, except that the apparent wording of al-Kashshaf requires that His words ﴿The sun and the moon by a reckoning﴾ be among the predicates, so consider this carefully.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 55, verses 7–8:

﴿And the sky — He raised it.﴾ That is, He created it raised from the beginning, not that it was lowered and then He raised it. The apparent meaning is that the raising refers to a physical, sensible elevation. It is also possible that it refers to something that includes both the physical and the figurative, by way of the general sense of metaphor (*majaz*), or by combining the literal and the figurative sense according to those who permit that. Its figurative raising is a raising in rank, because it is the source of God's rulings (*ahkam*) and decrees (*qada'ya*), the place where His commands descend, and the abode of His angels, Mighty and Majestic is He.

Abu al-Sammal read *wa-al-sama'a* (the sky) in the nominative case, as a beginning (*ibtida'*). There is no difficulty in this, because the sentence is then a nominal sentence (*jumla ismiyya*) conjoined to one like it. The difficulty lies in the accusative, since it would be governed by a hidden verb under the condition of the explanatory construction (*tafsir*), meaning "and He raised the sky," so that the sentence would be a verbal sentence (*jumla fi'liyya*). If it is conjoined to the major sentence ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, the two sentences differ, one nominal and one verbal, and this is contrary to what is preferable. If it is conjoined to the minor sentence ﴿prostrate﴾, it would have to be a predicate for "the star and the tree," like it, and that is not valid, since there is no pronoun in it referring back to them. The same applies to conjoining it to the major and minor sentence ﴿the sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾. Abu 'Ali answered by choosing the second option, and said: it is not required that what is conjoined to a thing must have the state of that thing taken into account. He cited the idiom of their saying, "girded with a sword and a spear" (*mutaqallidan saifan wa rumhan*). Some chose the first option, and the difference is acceptable when it carries a fine point (*nukta*). Al-Tibi said:

The apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿the sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾, to indicate that the original sense was: He set the sun and the moon in motion and made the star and the tree prostrate. So He turned to the meaning of the continuity of subjugation and submission in the first two sentences, and the meaning of emphasis in the last one. The discussion of the nominative and accusative when the conjunction is followed by a sentence with two possible readings is explained in the books of grammar (*nahw*).

﴿And He set the balance﴾: that is, He legislated justice and commanded it, by granting every one who is qualified his due, and giving every possessor of a right his right, until the affairs of the world were ordered and set right. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand," meaning they remained in the most eloquent order and the most perfect firmness. Some of them said: the meaning is the survival of those in them of the two weights (humans and jinn), for were it not for justice, the people of the earth would destroy one another. As for the exalted assembly (the angels), no dispute arises among them that would require judgment and justice, so their mention is for emphasis. What he chose is that the heavens and the earth, meaning the whole world, are intended, and there is no doubt that were it not for justice the world would not be ordered. The source of what this speaker said is his supposition that justice in the hadith means justice in judgment, for settling disputes and the like. It is not as he supposed; rather, what is meant is the justice of God Mighty and Majestic, and His giving every thing He created its due.

The explanation of the balance (*mizan*) in this sense is what is reported from Mujahid, al-Tabari, and most scholars. It is a metaphor for justice, a clear metaphor (*isti'ara tasrihiyya*). From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak it is reported that what is meant is that by which the measures of things are known, such as the known instrument, the known measure, and the like. The meaning, then, is that He created it placed and lowered upon the earth, such that He attached to it the rulings of His servants and their decrees sent down from the sky, and what He had them worship through equity and balance in their taking and giving. The prevailing view is that in this sense it is also a metaphor, through the use of the restricted for the general. It has also been said that it is a literal usage: the word was coined only for what by which measures are known, in whatever form and of whatever kind it is, and since people are accustomed to the familiar instrument, nothing else comes to their minds upon hearing the word *mizan*. It has also been said that what is meant is the familiar instrument, and the word is used literally there, but the claim that the word was coined for the general sense is not sound.

Those last two views are preferred, because what follows fits them better, and between "He set" (*wada'a*) and "raised" (*rafa'a*) there is an antithesis according to them. Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] read *wa-khaffada al-mizan* (and lowered the balance). The first reading is the most complete in benefit. So weigh that by the balance of your mind.

﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾: that is, lest you transgress in it, meaning in its right and its state, by overstepping and exceeding what ought to be observed in it. This is on the basis that *an* is a subordinating particle (*nasiba*), *la* is a negation, and the particle of cause (*lam al-'illa*) is implied, governed by the statement of the Exalted: "He set the balance." Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari allowed that *an* could be an explanatory particle (*tafsiriyya*) and *la* a prohibitive (*nahiyya*).

Abu Hayyan objected to this: no sentence containing the sense of saying has preceded it, and that is a condition for the validity of making *an* explanatory. It was answered that setting the balance does contain that, because it was through revelation and the informing of the messengers, peace be upon them. Some claimed that the explanatory reading is the only correct one, because there is no sense in "He set the balance so that you do not transgress in the balance," since the appropriate word would be "what is weighed" and the like. There is in this what is not hidden. In *al-Bahr* it is reported that Ibrahim read *wa-wad'a al-mizan* with a sukun on the *dad* and the genitive on *mizan*, so that *wad'* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) governed by what follows it. He did not specify whether *wad'* is nominative or accusative. If it is nominative, the apparent reading is that it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and "that you not transgress" is in the predicate position with the preposition implied. If it is accusative, the apparent reading is that its governing verb is implied: "and He did (the) setting of the balance, that you not transgress," or "and He set the setting of the balance, that you not transgress," and so on.

Abdullah read *la taṭghaw* (do not transgress) without *an*, with the intention of saying, meaning "saying" or something like it, not "say," as has been stated. The *la* is prohibitive, as shown by the jussive mood.

﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾: make your weighing just. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: this is a pointer to observing equity in all the actions and words that a person intends. It is reported from Mujahid that the meaning is: establish the tongue of the balance with justice when you are taking and giving. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: the establishing is by the hand, and the justice is by the heart. The apparent view is that this clause is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the negated clause before it, and that its being imperative (inshaʾiyyah) does no harm to this, while that clause is declarative (khabariyyah), because by being construed as a noun phrase it has been stripped of the sense of command. Some have made the first ﻻ (lā) a prohibitive in every case, out of eagerness for consistency. ﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾: that is, do not diminish it, for it is its right to be made level, since that is the purpose of its being set up. The word (al-mizan) is repeated without a pronoun, as the apparent style would require, to emphasise the injunction and to stress the command to use it and urge it. Indeed, in the three clauses there is a repetition of what has the same meaning, for this purpose.

It was read "wa-la tukhsirū" with a fatḥah on the tāʾ and a ḍammah on the sīn. Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Bilāl ibn Abī Burdah read it with a fatḥah on the tāʾ and a kasrah on the sīn. Ibn Jinni and the author of al-Lawāmiḥ related from Bilāl that he read it with fatḥah on both. Al-Zamakhshari explained this by saying that the original is "wa-la tukhsirū fī al-mizan," so the preposition was deleted and the verb was made to take a direct object, on the basis that the verb (khasira) has only come intransitively. Abu Hayyan objected that khasira has come transitively, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They have lost their souls﴾ [al-Anʿam: 12] and elsewhere, and ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]; so there is no need to claim deletion and conveyance. It was answered that if it is transitive here, then there must indeed be the assertion of deletion and conveyance, because the meaning on the deletion of the direct object would be: do not lose your souls in the balance, that is, do not be among those who lose them on the Day of Resurrection because of the balance, by not observing what is required in it. Al-Raghib permitted understanding the verse according to the well-known reading in a similar way. He said: the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient﴾, may be a pointer to seeking justice in weighing and abandoning injustice in what one deals in; and it may be a pointer to engaging in what will not make one a loser on the Day of Resurrection, and so one would be among those of whom He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whose scales are light﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 9; al-Muʾminun: 103; al-Qariʿah: 8]. It was also said: the meaning is on transitivity by postulating an annexed noun (muḍaf), that is, "the weighed item of the balance," or the balance is taken as a metaphor (majaz) for the thing weighed in it. ﴿And the earth — He laid it down for the creatures.﴾ [Wa-al-ard wada'aha] He created it laid down (mawdu'atan), lowered (makhfudatan) relative to the sky, as is observed. Al-Raghib said: "Wad' (placing down) here means bringing into existence and creating," and it seems his intention is what has been mentioned. It was also said: that is, lowering it while it is spread out (madhuwwatan) upon the water.

Given the assumption of the spreading (al-dahw), the apparent meaning is that there is no need to consider that He, glorified is He, created it in that state. Rather, it is not valid, because it was not created spread out; it was spread out afterwards, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Then, that its being upon the water is based on what is well known, that He, mighty and majestic is He, created the water before it, and created it, glorified is He, from its foam (zubd).

﴿For the creatures (lil-anam)﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said, according to Majma' al-Bahrayn, that it means all living beings (al-hayawan kulluhu). Al-Hasan said: humankind and jinn.

In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, it is only the children of Adam. I have not seen this specification attributed to anyone else, may Allah be pleased with him. In the Qamus: al-Anam means creation, or the jinn and humankind, or everything upon the face of the earth. It is possible that he meant that the intended sense here is that, based on the lam being for benefit (al-intifa'), and that it is carried upon complete benefit, which is more complete for humankind than for others. But the preferable view in my opinion is what was reported from him first. And Abu al-Sammal recited "wal-ardu" with a nominative (raf') vowel.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 11–13:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿In it is fruit﴾ and so on, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf musawwiq) serving to confirm what the preceding sentence conveyed, namely that the earth was laid out for the benefit of mankind. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) relating to the earth or to its pronoun; in that case the best reading is that the circumstantial element is the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur). ("Fruit," fakihah) is in the nominative, functioning as the subject, and it is indefinite (tanwin) to indicate abundance, as the context supports; that is, in it are many kinds of things by which one takes delight. ﴿And the palm tree, with its sheaths﴾: the sheaths (akmam) are the receptacles of the dates, namely the spathe (tal'), according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is the plural of kimm, with a kasrah on the kaf, though it may also be pronounced with a dammah; this applies to the "sheath" of fruit, whereas the "sheath" (kumm) of a shirt is pronounced with a dammah only. Alternatively, it means whatever is enclosed and covered, of fiber, palm frond, or spathe, for it is among the things that are benefited from, like the enclosed fruit and the heart of the palm (jummar) for example, and this view was preferred by those who preferred it. It has also been said that it refers to the species, and that this is permissible because their father was created from what has been mentioned. Al-salsal is dry clay that has a ringing sound (salsalah). Its root, as al-Raghib said, is the reverberation of sound from a dry object, and from this it is said: "salla al-mismar" (the nail rang). It has also been said that it is foul clay, from their saying: "salla al-lahm" (the meat became putrid). It is as if its original form was salsal, and one of the two lams was changed into a sad. What rules this out is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿like pottery﴾. Al-fakhkhar is al-khazaf, that is, clay that has been fired until it hardens, and it was named thus for its sound when struck, as if it were fashioned in the form of one who boasts greatly. God, exalted is He, created Adam, peace be upon him, from dust which He made into clay, then into black mud moulded (hama masnun), then into salsal. Therefore there is no contradiction between the verse that speaks of one of these and what has been stated about the other two.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 55, verses 22–23:**

﴿From them come forth the pearl﴾: the small pearls, ﴿and the coral﴾: the large ones. This was transmitted by ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face,

and by Mujahid. ʿAbd [al-Razzaq] transmitted it from al-Rabiʿ and a group including the two mentioned, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, through several chains, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Jarir also transmitted from him that he said: "*al-lu'lu'* (the pearl) is what is large of it, and *al-marjan* (the coral) is the small pearls."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "*al-marjan*" is the red bead, meaning the *busadh* (a type of coral), which is the well-known and familiar one. "*Al-lu'lu'*" includes both large and small. Furthermore, *al-lu'lu'* is a rare word pattern (*bina' gharib*). It was said that no more than five such words are known in the speech of the Arabs: *lu'lu'* itself, *al-ju'ju'* (the chest), a village in Bahrain, *al-du'du'* (the end of the month, or the night of the 25th, 26th or 27th, or the 28th or 29th, or the last three nights of it), and *al-bu'bu'* (with the letter *ba'*: the origin, the chief, the elegant one, the pupil of the eye, and the middle of a thing). *Al-yu'yu'* (with the letter *ya'*, the last letter) is a bird like the sparrowhawk. I have seen in the lexicons other words of this pattern, such as *al-dau'dau'* (the origin of a bird). *Al-nu'nu'* (with the letter *nun*) is one who frequently turns the eyeball, and the coward. From this is *shu'shu'*, the call of a donkey to water, and the driving of sheep and donkeys to go forward; or it is a call to sheep to eat or drink.

As for *al-marjan*, the author of *al-Qamus* mentioned it under the root *m-r-j* and did not mention anything indicating that it is a loanword. Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr*: it is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabicised. Ibn Duraid said: "I have not heard of a conjugated verb derived from it."

Talha read *al-lu'lu'i* with a kasra on the final *lam*. It is also read *al-lu'li*, with the final *hamza* changed to a sukun *ya'* after a kasra on the letter before it. Each of these is a dialect form.

Nafiʿ and Abu ʿAmr read *yakhruju* in the passive voice, from *ikhraj* (causing to come out). It is also read in the active voice, *yakhruju*, with *al-lu'lu'a wa al-marjana* in the accusative, meaning "Allah Most High brings forth."

A difficulty arises with the interpretation of the two seas as the sweet and the salt, rather than the seas of Persia and Rome. The problem is that what is observed is the emergence of the pearl and coral from one of them, which is the salt sea. So how does He say "from them both"? It is answered that since the two have met and become like one thing, it is permissible to say "they come forth from them," just as one says "they come forth from the sea," not from all of it but from part of it. Just as you say, "she came out of the town," though she came out from a quarter of it, indeed from one house among its houses. What belongs to one of two may be attributed to both, just as what proceeds from one of a group may be attributed to the group. Similar to this is what is in *al-Intisaf*: "*ʿala rajulin mina al-qaryatayni ʿazim*" (upon a great man from the two towns) [Az-Zukhruf: 31], and in accordance with what is reported from al-Zajjaj:

[Page 107]

﴿seven heavens in layers﴾ and ﴿made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 15–16]. It was also said that the two do not emerge except from the meeting-point of the sweet and the salt. But observation refutes this. It seems that whoever mentioned this together with what preceded did not mention it as a different opinion, but rather to strengthen the idea of unity, in which case the figurative link (*ʿalaqat al-tajawwuz*) is stronger.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: this is of the type of omission of the qualifier (*hadhf al-mudaf*), and the meaning is "it comes forth from one of them." He placed "from the two towns" in this category. In my view, this is a determination of meaning, not of grammatical structure (*taqdir maʿna la taqdir iʿrab*). Al-Rummani said: the sweet of them is like the stallion's seed for the salt, so it is like saying "the child comes forth from the male and the female," meaning through the two of them as intermediaries.

Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrima said: these things come about in the sea through the falling of rain, because in the month of Nisan the oysters receive rainwater with their mouths, and so they are formed from it, which is why they are scarce in times of drought. The pronoun in "from them both" is taken to refer to the two seas by way of the genus, and this is not needed, according to what Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that the intended "two seas" are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth.

Ibn Jubayr also transmitted something similar, through Ibn al-Mundhir, except that regarding the formation of the coral according to the interpretation of it as *busadh* from rainwater, like the pearl, there is some hesitation, even though they say it forms in Nisan. Some of the scholars said: the apparent meaning of the speech of Allah Most High takes precedence over the speech of people. Whoever knows that the pearl does not come forth from fresh water, let us grant that the divers only brought it out from the salt water. But why do you say that the oyster does not, by the command of Allah Most High, move from the fresh water to the salt water? Its emergence is possible, out of delight in the saltiness, just as a pregnant woman craves it in the early stages of her pregnancy, until, once it has come out, it cannot return. How can you be certain of what you have said, when many apparent earthly matters are hidden from merchants who have crossed deserts and roamed the lands? How then could something at the bottom of the sea be hidden from them? And Allah Most High knows best.

This is the view of the theosophist philosophers (al-mutalahhun) and the realized Sufis. However, the taste of the theosophists is that the relation of metaphor is that they have a particular relation to the presence of the Necessary Existence in various ways and diverse modes, and the paths to Allah, Exalted, are as numerous as the breaths of creatures. So existence, for them, is a real particular subsisting in itself, which cannot be conceived as accidental to anything or subsisting in anything. The application to the first view is to say: what is meant by the face which faces His direction, Exalted is He, is necessity by another, for the possible, even if it is truly existent according to the majority, its existence is derived from the Necessary by Essence, and the aspect of derivation is not the Essence itself nor any other of the directions and aspects, such as possibility, being caused, substantiality, accidentality, simplicity, composition, and the rest of the general matters, because each of these has the aspect of baseness. The natural disposition requires possibility, which is far removed from essential necessity and contrary to it. Rather, the nearby aspect of nobility, suitable for essential necessity, is the aspect of necessity by another. So this is a face which faces the direction of the Necessary and resembles it in being necessity, even if by another. For this reason the outpouring of existence follows it. However, the taste of the theosophists is that the relation of metaphor is that they have a particular relation to the presence of the Necessary Existence in various ways and diverse modes, and the paths to Allah, Exalted, are as numerous as the breaths of creatures. So existence, for them, is a real particular subsisting in itself, which cannot be conceived as accidental to anything or subsisting in anything. The meaning of the possible being existent is that it manifests Him and is a locus in which His light shines forth: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth" (24:35), and the possibles are like the various mirrors upon which the rays of the sun fall, and each of them takes on a colour that suits it. The taste of the realized Sufis is that the relation of metaphor is that they are like attributes subsisting in the Essence of the Necessary, Glorified is He, for in existence, according to their taste, there are not multiple essences, some necessary and some possible, but rather one essence which has many attributes, numerous modes, and renewed manifestations: "Say: Allah; then leave them" (6:91). It is well known that there is no difference between the two tastes.

The application to the first view is to say: what is meant by the face which faces His direction, Exalted is He, is necessity by another, for the possible, even if it is truly existent according to the majority, its existence is derived from the Necessary by Essence, and the aspect of derivation is not the Essence itself nor any other of the directions and aspects, such as possibility, being caused, substantiality, accidentality, simplicity, composition, and the rest of the general matters, because each of these has the aspect of baseness. The natural disposition requires possibility, which is far removed from essential necessity and contrary to it. Rather, the nearby aspect of nobility, suitable for essential necessity, is the aspect of necessity by another. So this is a face which faces the direction of the Necessary and resembles it in being necessity, even if by another. For this reason the outpouring of existence follows it. For this reason you hear them say: "The possible is what has not become necessary, so it does not come into existence."

The application to the second view is to say: the face which faces His direction, Exalted is He, is that particular relation which validates the application of the term "existent" to it, even if metaphorically. The meaning, then, is: "Everyone upon it is perishing": it is non-existent and it is not correct to apply the term "existent" to it, even metaphorically, except by considering the face which faces His direction, Exalted is He, that is, the particular relation to His Presence, Exalted is He, which is its being a manifestation of Him, Glorified is He.

The application to the third view is to say: what is meant by the face which faces His direction, Exalted is He, is that they are His modes and considerations, Exalted is He.

So the meaning is: "Everyone upon it" is non-existent in all faces and considerations, except from the face which faces His direction, Glorified is He, and the consideration which arises in relation to Him, Mighty and Majestic, namely that it is one of His affairs and one of His considerations, Majestic is His affair. So reflect, seeking help from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, that is, the monotheists declare Him free from likeness to His creation and affirm for Him what befits His majesty, Exalted is His majesty. This refers to His greatness in the hearts of those who know Him, Mighty and Majestic. Or, it refers to what is said of His affair: "How exalted You are, and how honoured You are," that is, He, Glorified is He, is the One who deserves that this be said of Him, whether or not it has been said. This refers to His perfection in Himself, considering that the perception falls short of reaching His eminence. Or, majesty and honour come from Him to the monotheists, so this refers to the act, that is, He ennobles the monotheists and honours them. The justification for the first explanation is that majesty is greatness, and greatness requires His exaltedness above existing things and entails that He, Glorified is He, is independent of them. Then it was attached to the reality. For this reason al-Jawhari said: "The greatness of a thing is its independence from other than it, and every one in need is contemptible." Al-Karmani said:

He, Exalted is He, has negative attributes, like "He has no partner" (6:163), and these are called attributes of majesty (sifat al-jalal), because they are rendered with "far above such and such, far above such and such." And His attributes of existence, like life and knowledge, are called attributes of honour (sifat al-ikram). There is room for reflection in this.

Apparently "Possessor" (dhu) is an adjective of "Face." The description with what has been mentioned implies, according to what some have mentioned, a reference to the fact that the perishing of "everyone upon it" does not diminish His affair, Mighty and Majestic, because He is the Absolutely Independent. It also indicates that He, Exalted is He, after their perishing, bestows upon the two weighty ones of the blessings of His generosity whatever He bestows, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The description of the Face with what has been described makes it unlikely that it means the righteous deed or the direction, as you have heard just now. It seems that whoever holds that view also says: "Possessor" (dhu) is the predicate of an omitted subject, which is a pronoun referring to the Lord, and it was originally an adjective of Him, then it was detached from being a follower. This is supported by what al-Tirmidhi related from Anas, and Imam Ahmad from Rabi'ah ibn Amir, as a raised hadith: "Persist in calling upon Him as 'O Possessor of Majesty and Honour'," that is, cling to it, be steadfast in it, and say it often and utter it in your supplications. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Do you know with what he supplicated?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." ﴿Then which of the bounties of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ This is because of what this verse implies, for passing away is a gateway to remaining, to eternal life, and to reward with everlasting blessing. Al-Tibi said: what is meant by the preceding verse is the necessary meaning of its content, because it is a metaphor for the coming of the time of recompense, and that is among the greatest blessings. For this reason, "Majesty and Honour" were specifically mentioned, because they indicate reward and punishment. What is meant by them is to frighten the servants and warn them against committing what entails punishment, and warning against such things is itself a blessing. For this reason the verse ﴿Then which of the bounties...﴾ etc. was ordered with "then" (fa) after it. But this is not so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verse 29–30:

﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾ entirely, for what they need in their essences, in origination and in continuance, and in all their states, a continuous asking, whether by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of condition. For they are all, in terms of their possible realities, wholly devoid of deserving existence and of what follows from it of perfections in any way, such that if the connection between them and the divine care (al-'inayah al-ilahiyyah) were severed, they would not smell the scent of existence at all. Thus they are, at every moment, askers.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Salih, concerning ﴿Everyone in the heavens asks Him﴾: mercy; and whoever is on the earth: forgiveness and provision. Ibn al-Mundhir also related from Ibn Jurayj that (it asks Him) — the angels, peace be upon them, ask for provision for the people of the earth, and forgiveness.

The people of the earth ask for both of them together, and what has preceded is more apt. There is no evidence for restriction.

The apparent reading is that the sentence is a new resumptive clause (isti'naf). It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿the Face﴾, and its governing element is ﴿remains﴾ (yabqa), meaning: He, glory be to Him, abides in this state, and His condition is not hidden from anyone who discerns. ﴿Every day﴾: every time of the times and every moment of the moments.

﴿He is in a matter﴾ of the matters, among which is giving what they asked, for He, exalted, never ceases to bring into being persons, to cause others to perish, to bring about states and to take away states, as His will requires, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms. Al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and a group related from Abu al-Darda', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning this verse: "Among His matters is that He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises a people and lowers others." Al-Bazzar added: "and answers one who calls."

It has also been said that Allah, exalted, has three hosts each day: a host from the loins (al-aslab) to the wombs, a host from the wombs to this world, and a host from this world to the graves. The apparent meaning is that the intent is to explain the multiplicity of His matters, exalted, in this world, so "every day" means every time of the times of this world.

Ibn 'Uyaynah said: With Allah, exalted, the age (al-dahr) is two days: one of them is the day which is the duration of this world, so His matter in it is command and prohibition, death and life. The second is the day which is the Day of Resurrection, so His matter, glory be to Him, in it is recompense and reckoning.

It is related from Muqatil that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, who said: "Allah, exalted, does not decide anything on the Sabbath," so He, mighty and majestic, refuted them with this. Abd Allah ibn Tahir asked al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl about reconciling this verse with what is authentically related, that the pen has dried with what is to be until the Day of Resurrection. He said: "They are matters He manifests, not matters He initiates."

﴿Every day﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and its governing element is the governing element of His saying, exalted, ﴿in a matter﴾, and it is the stable element that is omitted (thabit al-mahdhuf). So it is as if it were said: He is established in the matter of every day.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ — of what He grants to fulfil your asking, and what He brings out for you with His two hands from the hidden place of non-existence, moment after moment.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 31–32]

﴿We shall attend to you﴾. Linguistically, *al-faragh* (freeing oneself) presupposes a prior occupation.

Freeing oneself for something also presupposes that it comes afterward. God, glorified is He, is not preoccupied by one affair to the exclusion of another. So the ending of the affairs referred to by His words ﴿Every day He is upon some affair﴾ (55:29), from the Day of Resurrection onward, is made to be a single matter, which is the recompense of the responsible persons. This is a figurative representation of freeing oneself for them, because one who abandons his occupations for a single task is said to have *faragha lahu* and *ilayhi* (he devoted himself to it). So God likened the state of these people, and His dealing with them in their recompense alone, to the state of one for whom one has freed oneself. The explicit, subordinate metaphor (*al-isti'arah al-tasrihiyyah al-tab'iyyah*, a metaphor in which the verb itself is borrowed) is permissible in ﴿sanafrugh﴾, with the meaning "We shall only take up your recompense." The shared element is taking up the recompense alone and freeing oneself from all other concerns for one thing, namely that the meaning is that one thing.

It has also been said that the intended meaning is full concentration on punishment and vexation. Freeing oneself for something is often used in threats, as if one had freed oneself from everything else for its sake, so nothing remains for him to occupy himself with except it. This indicates the concentration mentioned. It is an allusion (*kinayah*) with regard to one to whom it can apply, and a figurative usage (*majaz*) with regard to other than him, as in the case we are discussing.

Perhaps the meaning intended by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak in their saying, as Ibn Jarir reported from them, is that this is a warning from God to His servants of what has been mentioned. The address in it has been said to be to the criminals, but this was objected to on the grounds that the call that follows rules it out. Yes, the ones intended by the threat are them. It has also been said: there is no barrier to threatening everyone. Furthermore, this threat refers only to what will happen on the Day of Resurrection. As for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah, that it is possible that this is a warning of the punishment of this world, which one hardly pays attention to, it has been said:

That *faragha* has the meaning of *qasada* (to intend). He cited as evidence what Ibn al-Anbari recited from Jarir:

*Now, since you have turned to Numayr, this is the time when you were a torment to them.*

That is, you intended them. Al-Nahhas recited:

*You turned to the shackled slave in the anklet.*

In a hadith: "I will surely attend to you, you wicked one," which the Prophet (ﷺ) said addressing Azabb al-'Aqabah on the day of its pledge, meaning: I will surely intend to nullify your affair. This was reported from al-Khalil, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'. Apparently, they took what is in the verse to be of this kind, so the meaning then is that the will is directly attached to their recompense.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Haywah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *sayafrugh* with the third-person masculine prefix (ya-). Qatadah and al-A'raj read *sanafrugh* with the first-person plural prefix (na-, the royal "we") and a fatha on the ra, the imperfect of *faringa* with a kasra, which is the dialect of Tamim, just as *sanafrugh* in the common reading is the imperfect of *faraga* with a fatha, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. Abu al-Sammal and 'Isa read *sanifrugh* with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the ra, which, according to Abu Hatim, is the dialect of Lower Mudar. Al-A'mash and Abu Haywah, in a variant from them, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah and al-Za'faranI read

*sayufraghu* with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the ra, in the passive voice. 'Isa also read *sunafrigh* with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ra. Al-A'raj also read *sayafragh* with a fatha on the ya and the ra, and this is a dialect. It was also read *saafrigh* with the hamzah of the first-person singular. Ubayy read *sanafrugh ilaykum*, governing it with *ila*. It has been said that this is for the purpose of implying intention, or that the verb is construed to carry its meaning: ﴿we shall attend to you﴾, intending you.

﴿O you two weighty ones﴾: the two weighty ones are mankind and the jinn, from the "weight" (*thiql*) of a beast, which is what is loaded upon it. The earth has been made like a load, and mankind and the jinn are its two loads, and whatever else exists is, on this view, like an addition. Other than one has said: they were named so because of their heaviness upon the earth, or because of the gravity of their judgment, their worth and the greatness of their station. Anything of great value that people compete for is called a *thiql*. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am leaving among you the two weighty things: the Book of God and my family (*'itrah*)." It has also been said that they were named so because they are burdened with obligation, and from al-Hasan: because of their weight with sins.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ Among these favours is the warning of what you will encounter on the Day of Resurrection, so that you may be cautioned against what leads to a bad reckoning.

﴿to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning to go out from the sides of the heavens and the earth, fleeing from God, Exalted, and escaping His decree, glorified be He. ﴿Then pass through﴾ means go out from them and save yourselves from His punishment, Mighty and Majestic. The command is for incapacitation (ta'jiz). ﴿You will not pass through﴾ means you will not be able to pass through ﴿except with authority﴾, that is, with power and dominance. You are far from that, a thousand thousand stations away.

When the jinn and humankind see them, they flee, but they do not go in any direction without finding that the angels have surrounded it. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 39–40:**

﴿So on that Day﴾: that is, the Day when the sky is split open, as has been mentioned.

﴿No one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾: because they are recognized by their marks (*simahum*), and this refers to one station. What indicates questioning, such as the verse ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr 15:92], refers to another station. This was said by Ikrimah and Qatadah. It is said that the station of questioning is at the reckoning, and the absence of questioning is at the departure from the graves. Ibn Abbas said: wherever questioning is mentioned, it is questioning of rebuke and confirmation, and wherever it is negated, it is pure inquiry about the sin. It was also said that what is negated is questioning about the sin itself, and what is affirmed is questioning about the motive behind it. You know that the verses contain what indicates questioning about the sin itself.

Al-Tabarsi related from al-Rida, may Allah be pleased with him, that whoever believes in the truth and then sins without repenting will be punished in the *barzakh* (the intermediate state between death and resurrection), and will come out on the Day of Resurrection with no sin about which he will be asked. By my life, al-Rida did not say this. Interpreting the verse in this way is not something to be considered with the eye of al-Rida, as is clear. The pronoun in *dhanbihi* ("his sin") refers to *al-ins* (man), and it is higher in rank because it is the substitute for the subject (*na'ib 'an al-fa'il*). Its singular form is based on the wording. It was also said that since the intended meaning is an individual from among mankind, it is as if it were said: "No one among humans or jinn will be asked about his sin." Al-Hasan and Amr ibn Ubayd read *wa-la ja'anna* ("and not a jinn") with a hamza, to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*), although it is on its usual rule. The verse ﴿Then which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ is treated in the same way as what was heard in its context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 41–42:

﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that functions as a justification (ta'lil) for the negation of questioning. "Al-mujrimun" (the criminals) — it has been said that it is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, to indicate that what is meant is some of mankind and some of the jinn, who are the criminals. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. As for "simahum" (their marks), according to what has been narrated from al-Hasan, they are the blackness of faces and the blueness of eyes. It has also been said that they are the dejection and sorrow that overcomes them, and it is permissible that they be other matters, such as blindness, muteness, and deafness.

Hammad ibn Sulayman read "bi-simaihim" (by their marks). ﴿So they will be seized by the forelocks﴾: "nawasi" is the plural of "naseyah" (forelock), which is the front of the head. ﴿And the feet﴾: the plural of "qadam," which is the well-known foot of a man. The "ba'" here is for instrumentality (lil-alah), like it in "akhadhta bi-khitam al-dabbah" (you took hold of the halter of the animal), and the prepositional phrase is the deputy of the subject.

Abu Hayyan said: the "ba'" is for transitivity (lil-ta'diyah), and the verb is construed with the meaning of what is transitive by it, i.e., "fa-yusahabu bi-n-nawasi" (so they will be dragged by the forelocks), etc. In this there is a discussion. The apparent sense of the words of more than one scholar is that the "al-" (the definite article) is a substitute for the pronominal suffix of the genitive, i.e., "bi-nawasihim wa-aqdamihim" (by their forelocks and their feet). Abu Hayyan explicitly stated this, saying: the "al-" in both is a substitute for the pronoun according to the Kufan school, while the pronoun is elided according to the Basran school, i.e., "bi-n-nawasi wa-l-aqdami minhum" (by the forelocks and the feet of them). You know that the dispute between the people of the two cities concerns when the pronoun is needed for linkage, and there is no need for it here. Yes, the meaning is according to the pronoun. As for the manner of this seizing, according to what has been narrated from al-Dahhak, it is that the king gathers one of them between his forelock and his two feet with a chain from behind his back, then breaks his back and throws him into the Fire. It has also been said: the angels, peace be upon them, seize some of them by dragging them by the forelock and some of them by dragging them by the foot. It has also been said: the angels, peace be upon them, drag them at times by seizing the forelocks and at times by seizing the feet, so the "wa" (and) is in the sense of "aw" (or) which is for division, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The concealment of the agent is because it is almost determined. It has been said: it is for signifying His greatness.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi (?) and Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in "Sifat al-Nar" transmitted from Anas, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the angels of Hell were created a thousand years before Hell was created. Every day they increase in strength over their strength, until they seize those whom they seize by the forelocks and the feet." ﴿Then which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ Concerning it, the same as what preceded is said.

As for the manner of this seizing, according to what has been narrated from al-Dahhak, it is that the king gathers one of them between his forelock and his two feet with a chain from behind his back, then breaks his back and throws him into the Fire. It has also been said: the angels, peace be upon them, seize some of them by dragging them by the forelock and some of them by dragging them by the foot. It has also been said: the angels, peace be upon them, drag them at times by seizing the forelocks and at times by seizing the feet, so the "wa" (and) is in the sense of "aw" (or) which is for division, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The concealment of the agent is because it is almost determined. It has been said: it is for signifying His greatness.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi (?) and Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in "Sifat al-Nar" transmitted from Anas, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the angels of Hell were created a thousand years before Hell was created. Every day they increase in strength over their strength, until they seize those whom they seize by the forelocks and the feet." ﴿Then which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ Concerning it, the same as what preceded is said.

"And His saying, ﴿This is Hell which the criminals deny⁠﴾, is the object of an implied speech-verb, conjoined to His saying (they are seized…) etc., meaning: and it will be said, 'This is…' etc. Or it is a resumptive clause (mustaʼnaf) answering the question 'What will be said to them?', since this is a context of rebuke and reproach. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the people of the forelocks (aṣḥab al-nawāṣī), based on the assumption that the original is 'their forelocks' or 'the forelocks are from them.' What comes between is a parenthetical interjection (iʻtirāḍ) on the first and the last. The original wording would have been ﴿which you denied⁠﴾, but it was changed, for the reason mentioned, to indicate the continuity of that denial and to clarify the basis of their rebuke and its cause.

﴿They go about between it⁠﴾, i.e., they move back and forth between its fire ﴿and between scalding water⁠﴾, i.e., hot water ﴿intensely heated⁠﴾, i.e., reaching the utmost limit of its heat in its boiling and cooking. Qatadah said: "The scalding water has been boiling since Allah created Hell, and the criminal is punished by alternating between being roasted in the fire and drinking the scalding water." It was also said: they are burned in the fire and scalding water is poured over their heads. It was also said: when they seek relief from the fire, their relief is made to be the scalding water. ﴿Wa-liman khaafa maqaama rabbihi﴾ and so on. This begins the enumeration of the blessings that will be bestowed in the Hereafter. (*Maqaam*) is a mimi verbal noun (*masdar mimi*) meaning standing (*qiyaam*), in the genitive construction with the agent: that is, ﴿for the one who fears﴾ the standing of his Lord, His being watchful over him, observing him, and guarding his affairs. Here *al-qiyaam* has the same sense as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul for what it has earned [like those who have no partners]?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. This is related from Mujahid and Qatadah. Alternatively, it is a noun of place, meaning the place where creatures stand on the Day of Resurrection for reckoning. The annexation to Him, exalted is He, is then a *lam* of specification (*idafah ikhtisasiyyah*), because sovereignty on that day belongs to Him alone, in reality, while the apparent and the creatures stand before Him, awaiting what will descend upon them from Him, majestic is His glory, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. Some have claimed that the annexation in this sense is for the slightest connection, but this is nothing. It has also been said: the meaning is ﴿for the one who fears﴾ his station before his Lord, with *maqaam* being a masdar or a noun of place, and it belongs to the fearer himself, and its annexation to the Lord is because it is in His presence, exalted is He. It is thus like their saying: *shaatun raqoodu al-halb* (a ewe that lies down at milking). Here *'inda* (with/at) means "at" according to the Kufans, i.e., lying down at the milking, and means *al-lam* according to the majority of grammarians, as the commentators of *al-Tashil* have explicitly stated. It is not for the slightest connection, as also claimed. Moreover, the meaning of "presence" here is clear enough. It is also permitted that the annexation be superfluous (*muqhaman*), by way of metonymy (*kinayah*), so that the meaning is: ﴿for the one who fears his Lord﴾, but by an eloquent demonstrative method. Similar to this is the verse of al-Shammakh:

*I startled the sand grouse with it and drove away from it the station of the wolf, like the cursed man.*

This is the more apparent view according to what the author of *al-Kashf* mentioned. The apparent meaning is that for every single individual among those who fear: ( **two gardens** ). It has been said:

One of them is his dwelling and the place where his beloved ones visit him, and the other is the dwelling of his spouses and servants. Al-Jubba'i took this view. It has also been said: two gardens, one inside his palace and one outside it. It has also been said: two dwellings, moving from one to the other, so that the causes of his enjoyment are abundant and the fruits of his honor appear. And how can this be the case for one who goes around between the fire and a boiling, scalding water?

It is also permitted to say: one garden for his belief and one garden for his deed; or one garden for performing acts of obedience and one garden for abstaining from sins; or one garden in which he is rewarded and another that is granted to him by grace; or one of them spiritual and the other physical. There is no doubt that the following attributes are apparent in the physical sense.

Muqatil said: the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Delight. It has also been said: the meaning is that for each of the two fearers among you (both of you) there are two gardens: one garden for the fearing human and one garden for the fearing jinn, since the address is to both groups. This, in my view, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the reports contain what refutes it. For al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* related from al-Hasan that there was a young man in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who was devoted to the mosque and worship. A slave-girl fell in love with him and came to him in seclusion and spoke to him, and his soul was tempted by that, so he gave a great sob and fainted. His paternal uncle came and carried him to his house. When he came to, he said: "O uncle, go to 'Umar, convey my greetings to him and say to him: what is the reward for one who fears the station of his Lord?" So he went and informed 'Umar, while the young man had given another great sob and died. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, stood over him and said: "For you are two gardens, for you are two gardens."

Fear (*al-khawf*), in origin, is the anticipation of something disliked upon a presumed or known sign, and its opposite is security. Al-Raghib said: "The fear of Allah, exalted is He, does not mean what comes to mind of terror, like feeling fear of a lion, but it means refraining from sins and seeking out acts of obedience. For this reason it was said: one who has not abandoned sins is not counted as fearing." This is supported by the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the fearer here is, as Ibn Jarir related from him, one who mounts obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and abandons His disobedience.

As for the saying of Mujahid: "He is the man who intends a sin, then remembers Allah, exalted is He, and so abandons the sin," the apparent view is that this is an interpretation by a necessary consequence (*tafsir bi-al-lazim*). It may be said that committing a sin may coexist with fear of Allah, exalted is He, as when his soul overcomes him so that he does it while fearing His punishment for it. This is corroborated by what Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and a group related from Abu al-Darda', that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, recited this verse: ﴿And for whoever fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾. So I said: "And even if he commits adultery and even if he steals, O Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The second time: ﴿And for whoever fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾." So I said: "And even if he commits adultery and even if he steals?" He said: "The third time: ﴿And for whoever fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾." So I said: "And even if he commits adultery and even if he steals?" He said: "Yes, and even if the nose of Abu al-Darda' is rubbed in the dust."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related through al-Jiriri, from his brother, who said: "I heard Muhammad ibn Sa'd reciting: ﴿And for whoever fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾ — 'and even if he commits adultery and even if he steals.' So I said: 'It does not contain "and even if he commits adultery and even if he steals."' He said: 'I heard Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, recite it thus, so I recite it thus until I die.'"

Some have stated that the intended sense of fear in the verse is its most intense degree, so reflect on this.

Concerning these two gardens, there has come from the hadith of 'Iyad ibn Ghanm, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The breadth of each one of them is a journey of a hundred years."

The verse, according to what is related from Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Shawdhab, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* related from 'Ata' that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned one day and reflected on the Resurrection, the scales, Paradise and Hell, the rows of the angels, the folding up of the heavens, the levelling of the mountains, the overthrowing of the sun, and the scattering of the stars. Then he said: "I wish I had been one of these green plants, that a beast would come to me and eat me, and that I had not been created." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And for whoever fears the station of his Lord are two gardens﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 47–48:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Both of them having many branches (dhawatā afnān).﴾ "Dhawatā" is an attribute (ṣifah) of "jannatān" (two gardens). What lies between them (wa-mā baynahumā) is an interjected clause (i'tirāḍ) placed between them as an alert (tanbīhan) that denying each of the qualified noun and the qualifier necessitates reproach and rebuke. It is also permissible for it to be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada' muqaddar), meaning "they are two possessors of branches." In either case, it is the dual of "dhāt" in the sense of "ṣāḥibah" (possessor). For its dual there are two forms: "dhātā" according to its own form, which is the more analogical (al-aqyas), just as its masculine is dualized as "dhawā"; and the other form, "dhawātā," by returning it to its original root, since the dual restores things to their roots. They have said:

The original of dhāt is dhawāt, but the waw was dropped for lightness and to distinguish the singular from the plural. The dual indicates the return of the waw in it to the root of the singular, and it is not the dual of the plural as is mistakenly supposed. Its full explanation is in the chapter on the dual in the commentary on al-Tashīl (Sharḥ al-Tashīl).

As for "al-afnān": it is either the plural of "fann" in the sense of "kind" (nawʿ), which is why it has come to be used in common usage in the sense of "science" (ʿilm), meaning two gardens possessing kinds of trees and fruits. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and upon it is the verse of the poet:

"And from every kind of delight and youth I enjoyed myself, while life was green and fresh."

Or it is the plural of "fanan," which is what is thin and soft of the branches, as Ibn al-Jawzi said; it may also be explained as "ghuṣn" (branch). It has been construed as a loose usage (tasāmuḥ), and its specification by mention, although they are also possessors of stalks, leaves and fruits, is because it is the branches that put forth leaves and bear fruit; from them the shades extend and from them the fruits are gathered. Thus in the description there is an implicit reference to both (tadhkīr), as if it were said: "possessors of" fruits and shades, but by way of metonymy (kināyah), which is more concise and more eloquent. Its explanation as "branches," on the basis that it is the plural of "fanan," is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jarir narrated it from Mujahid. Abu Hayyan said: "This is preferable, because the pattern afʿāl occurs more in fiʿl than in fiʿl with a sukūn on the ʿayn, as in fann." It is pluralized as "funūn."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 49–50:

﴿Then which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿In both of them are two springs, flowing.﴾ "Flowing" (ṣifah ukhrā li-jannatān, aw khabar thānin lil-mubtada' al-muqaddar): this is another attribute of "two gardens," or a second predicate of an implied subject, meaning: in each of them there is a spring flowing with pure water. One of the two springs is called al-Tasnim, and the other al-Salsabil. This is narrated from al-Hasan. ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi said: "two springs" means one of them is of water that does not change (ghayr āsin), and the other is of wine, delicious to those who drink it. It was also said: "two springs" of water, "flowing" wherever their owner wishes, from the high and low places of a mountain of musk. And from Ibn ʿAbbas: "two springs" are like the worldly life many times over, "flowing" with increase and honor over the people of Paradise.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 51–52:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are two kinds of every fruit.﴾ Two kinds: one familiar, and one strange that they did not know in the world. Or, fresh and dry, and its dry kind is not lacking in excellence and goodness compared with its fresh kind.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding this verse: "There is no fruit in this world, sweet or bitter, but it is in Paradise, even the colocynth (ḥanẓal)." This is also reported in al-Bahr from Ibn ʿAbbas, except that it is sweet. The sentence is like the sentence that precedes it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 53–54:**

﴿فَبِأيِّ آلاءِ رَبِّكُما تُكَذِّبانِ﴾ *(So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?)*

﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ *(reclining)* is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of His words, ﴿وَلِمَنْ خافَ﴾ *(and for him who fears)*. It is in the plural, for the sake of the meaning after the singular, and not for the sake of the wording. It is said that the governing verb is omitted, meaning "they enjoy themselves while reclining." It is also said that it is an object (*maf'ul bihi*) with the implied verb "I mean" (*a'ni*). Reclining is one of the attributes of those who live in luxury, indicating physical health and a free heart. The meaning is that they recline in their dwellings ﴿عَلى فُرُشٍ بَطائِنُها مِن إسْتَبْرَقٍ﴾ *(on couches whose linings are of brocade)*, meaning thick silk brocade.

Ibn Mas'ud said, as related from him by a group of narrators and authenticated by al-Hakim: "You have been informed of the linings, so how about the outer surfaces?" It is also said that their outer surfaces are of *sundus* (fine silk), from Ibn Jubayr, or of solid light. There is a hadith: "of light that shines." If it is authentic, it is to be stopped at (i.e., accepted as a limit and not exceeded).

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about ﴿بَطائِنُها مِن إسْتَبْرَقٍ﴾: "What then are the outer surfaces?" He said: "That is among what Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿فَلا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ ما أُخْفِيَ لَهم مِن قُرَّةِ أعْيُنٍ﴾ *(No soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes)* [As-Sajdah: 17]." Al-Hasan said: "The linings are the outer surfaces," and this was narrated from Qatada. Al-Farra' said: "The lining may be the outer surface, and the outer surface the lining, because each of them may be the face (the visible side), and the Arabs say: 'This is the back of the sky' and 'This is the belly of the sky.'" The correct view is that here the linings are the opposite of the outer surfaces, in the well-known sense.

Abu Haywa recited *furshin* (فُرْشٍ) with a sukun on the *ra'*. Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: Abdullah recited: "*sururin* (سُرُرٍ) and *furshin* whose linings are of brocade."

It has also been said: it refers to the cushions (furush). Abu Hayyan said: this is a good view, close in its derivation. It has been objected that what suits "the cushions" is "upon" (ʿala), and it has been answered that He likened their settling upon the cushions to the containment of the contained in the container, and chose this to indicate that most of their state is settled upon them. It may also be said: the use of the container-form (ẓarfiyya) signals that when one sits on these cushions, the place of the sitter sinks in them and what surrounds him rises, until he almost disappears into them, as is seen in the cushions of pampered kings, whose stuffing is ostrich feathers or the like. It has also been said:

The pronoun refers to the favours enumerated: the two gardens, the two springs, the fruits, and the cushions, and the ones with them, and the meaning includes ﴿women restraining their gaze﴾, i.e., women who restrict their gaze to their husbands and do not look at anyone else; or who restrict the glance of the one looking at them from passing to others. Ibn Rashiq said regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Of the women restraining their gaze, if a mite from the dust crawled upon the soft silk of hers, it would leave a mark."*

He meant by "restraining their gaze" that their eyelids are lowered, their glance is cast down, not looking into the distance, and not looking at anyone other than their husband. It may also mean that the glance of the beholder does not pass beyond them, as in the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

*"And a waist in which the eyes are fixed, as if upon it is a belt made of a jeweled cord."*

End of quotation, so do not be heedless. Most scholars adopt the first of the two meanings we have mentioned. Indeed, some reports indicate that it is a Prophetic explanation.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning this: "They do not look at anyone but their husbands." If this is authentic, the restriction of the gaze should be understood in this sense. In some reports, one of them says to her husband: "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you. All praise is due to God who made me your wife and made you my husband."

The word *al-tarf* (the glance) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is in the singular.

﴿No human has touched them before them, nor any jinn.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: no human before their husbands has deflowered them, nor any jinn. In this there is an indication that the pronoun in "before them" refers to the husbands, and this is supported by "women restraining their gaze". In al-Bahr it is said that it refers to whoever the pronoun in "reclining" refers to. The original meaning of *al-tamth* (deflowering) is the flow of blood, which is why menstruation is called *tamth*. Then it was applied to the intercourse with virgins, because of the flow of blood in it. It has also been said: then it was generalized to every intercourse, and this is what is related here from ʿIkrima. Most scholars took the first view. It has also been said that the expression with this word indicates that they are found as virgins each time they are had intercourse with. The negation of their deflowering by humans is clear. As for the negation regarding the jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: jinn may have intercourse with human women along with their husbands, when the husband has not mentioned the name of God, exalted is He. So here He negated all who have intercourse with them. It has also been said:

There is no need for this, since it is enough for the negation of deflowering by jinn that it is possible for them. There is no doubt in the possibility that a jinn has intercourse with a human woman without her husband, who does not mention the name of God, being present. This is supported by what Abu ʿUthman Saʿid ibn Dawud al-Zubaydi related: a group of people from Yemen wrote to Malik asking him about marrying jinn, and they said: "There is a man here from the jinn who claims that he wants what is lawful." It is also possible that all the houris are one kind, and the jinn among them is given one of them, but in that mode of existence she is different from her in this mode of existence. What the believer is given, whether human or jinn, of the houris is something suitable for him, which his soul desires. The reality of that mode of existence is beyond what comes to mind.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And besides them there are two gardens.﴾ Here "two gardens" is a *mubtada'* (subject) and a *khabar* (predicate). Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 55, verses 63–64:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Dark green﴾ is an attribute of *jannatan* (two gardens). The interjection (*i'tiraD*) was placed between them to draw attention to what preceded it, namely that denying each of the qualified and the qualifier alike deserves rebuke and censure. Alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are dark green." *Mudhammatan* derives from *al-dahma* (darkness), which, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is originally the blackness of the night. It is also used to describe the blackness of a horse, and it may be used to describe the full green of a colour, just as green is used when the green is not complete. This is because the two colours are close to each other. It is said: *ادْهامَّ ادْهِيمامًا* (*idhhamma idhhimamān*), so he is *مُدْهامٌّ* (*mudhammmmun*, on the pattern *muf'āll*), when it has turned black or its greenness has intensified. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and a group of others interpreted it here as *خَضْراوانِ* (*khaḍrāwān*, meaning "two very green ones").

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Ayyub, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Prophet ﷺ about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿dark green﴾, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Khaḍrāwān'" (very green).

The meaning is that they are intensely green, and when greenness becomes intense, it inclines towards blackness. This is from the abundance of water, as was narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and Abu Salih.

It has been said that describing these two gardens with what has been mentioned indicates that what predominates in them is vegetation and fragrant plants spread over the surface of the earth. Likewise, describing the two foremost gardens as *ذَواتا أفْنانٍ* (*dhawātā afnān*, "possessing branches") indicates that what predominates in them is trees, since trees are described as having branches, while vegetation is described as having intense greenness. Restricting each of the two descriptions to one of these matters indicates what has been mentioned.

Based on this, these two gardens are lower in rank and status than the first two. How could they not be, since a garden abundant in shade and fruit is higher and more precious than a garden scant in shade and fruit? Whoever holds that these two gardens are superior, even though the description of greenness is specific to vegetation, and even though it is more prevalent than describing trees with it, will note that people often say, when praising an orchard, "its trees are green and luxuriant." This is more evident in praising it as one that has fruit with branches. It also indicates an abundance of water, concern for its condition, and its distance from withering and destruction.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 67–68:**

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ ﴿In them is fruit, and palm trees and pomegranates.﴾ He conjoined the last two to fruit in the way that Jibril and Mikal (peace be upon them) are conjoined to the angels, to show their excellence. It has also been said that they are in this world, since they were not exclusively for enjoyment: the date palm's produce is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is both fruit and medicine. So they were conjoined to fruit as a separate kind. Yet everything in Paradise is for enjoyment, since it is pure pleasure. From this, Imam Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: if someone swears that he will not eat fruit and then eats a pomegranate or fresh dates, he does not break his oath (hanth, the legal violation of an oath). His two companions disagreed with him. Moreover, the palm trees and pomegranates of Paradise are beyond what we know.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and others narrated from Ibn Abbas: "The palm trees of Paradise: their trunks are green emerald, their karanif (the fibrous bases of the fronds) are red gold, their palm fronds are the clothing of the people of Paradise, from which are their cut garments and their robes, and their fruit is like large jars, whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, and softer than butter, and it has no seed (ajam)." Its ruling is the ruling of a marfu' report (one traced back to the Prophet ﷺ).

In a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Its roots are silver, its trunks are silver, its fronds are garments, and its produce is fresh dates, etc."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir narrated from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I looked at Paradise and saw that a pomegranate among its pomegranates is like a saddled camel." This praise, outwardly, falls short of the praise in His words in the two earlier gardens: ﴿In both of them are two kinds of every fruit.﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 52]. Those who hold that these two are superior say that the tanwin in "fakihah" (fruit) is for generalization (ta'mim), by the context, similar to what is said of His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented.﴾ [At-Takwir: 14]. So the meaning is in effect "in them is every fruit." The noble text goes beyond this by including an indication of the praise of some of its kinds.

Imam al-Razi said: "Here 'ma' is like His words: ﴿In both of them are two kinds of every fruit.﴾ This is because fruits are of earthly and tree kinds: earthly ones like melons and other cultivated plants, and tree ones like the palm and others. So He said ﴿dark green﴾ for the kinds of greenery in which there are earthly fruits, and in which there are also tree fruits. He, glory be to Him, mentioned from them two kinds: fresh dates and pomegranates, because they are opposites. One is sweet and the other sour; one is hot and the other cold; one is a fruit and food and the other is a fruit; one is from the fruits of hot lands and the other from the fruits of cold lands; one has trees that are extremely tall and the other does not; one has its edible part exposed and its inedible part hidden, and the other is the reverse. So they are like two opposites. Indicating the two extremes includes indicating what lies between them, as in His words: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests.﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 17]." End of quotation. But the first view is perhaps more preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 69–70:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are good [women], excellent [in character and beauty]﴾ is another attribute of ﴿two gardens﴾, or a second predicate of the omitted subject, like the sentence before it.

It is also permissible that it be a new sentence (mustaʼnafah), and the discussion of the plural pronoun here is like the discussion of it in His saying: ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾ [al-Rahman: 56].

(Khayrat) Abu Hayyan said: it is the plural of khayrah, a descriptive noun patterned on fiʻlah from khayr (good), just as they formed sharrah from sharr (evil). Al-Zamakhshari said: its origin is khayyirat with a shaddah, which was lightened, as in his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "hayyinun layyinun" (gentle and soft). The plural of khayyir in the sense of akhyar (better) does not take this form, for one does not say khayyirun or khayyirat; perhaps this is because the basic form of the comparative does not take a plural, especially when indefinite. Bakr ibn Habib, Abu ʻUthman al-Nahdi and Ibn Muqsim recited khayyirat with a doubled yaʼ, and this supports that its origin is so. It is also reported from Abu ʻAmr: khayarat with a fatha on the yaʼ, as if it were the plural of khaʼirah, pluralised on the pattern fiʻlah.

﴿Beautiful﴾ (ḥisan): it was said, meaning beautiful in character and in form.

ʻAbd al-Razzaq, ʻAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah that he said concerning the verse: ﴿khayrat﴾ refers to manners, and ﴿ḥisan﴾ to faces. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported the same from Umm Salamah, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).
