**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 75–76:**

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿reclining﴾. It has been said that it is by the implied verb "they enjoy themselves, reclining," or "I mean, reclining." The pronoun refers to the people of the two gardens, indicated by mention of them. ﴿On green cushions﴾: *rafraf* is a generic noun (*ism jins*) or a collective noun (*ism jam'*), whose singular is *rafrafah*. On both readings it is valid to describe it with the words of the Exalted: ﴿green﴾. Some have made it a plural of this description, but it is not hidden that the status of the description does not depend on that construction. Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak interpreted it in the verse as *fudul al-mahabis*, which are what is spread over the back of a bed for sleeping on. Al-Jawhari said: *al-rafraf* are green garments from which *al-mahabis* (canopies or bed-coverings) are made, and its derivation is from *raff*, meaning "to rise up." Al-Hasan said, as transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir and others from him, that they are carpets (*busut*).

It is also transmitted from Asim al-Jahdari that they are cushions (*wasa'id*), and this is also related from al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan. Al-Jubba'i said: raised bedding (*furush murtafi'ah*). It has been said: what hangs down from the bedsteads of fine garments. Al-Raghib said: a kind of garment likened to gardens. Ibn Jarir and a group transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: *al-rafraf* are the gardens of Paradise. And he transmitted from Abd ibn Humayd something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is, as in *al-Bahr*, from *raff al-nabt*, meaning plants that flourish and are beautiful. It is also said that *rafraf* is any wide garment, and the thin silk brocade garments, and the edges of a tent or pavilion that rest on the ground, below the guy-ropes and pegs. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that this meaning has been said here, but in it there is something (to consider).

﴿And of 'abqari﴾: it is a relative adjective (*mansub*) to *'Abqar*, which the Arabs claim is the name of the land of the jinn, so they attribute to it every wondrous and rare thing among carpets and other things. Its meaning is therefore "the marvelous, rare thing." From this is what came concerning Umar al-Faruq, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen an *'abqari* who fabricates a fabrication (*fariyah*)." Because that relative sense has been forgotten, it has been said that it is not a relative adjective but is like *kursi* and *bukhti*, as transmitted from Qutrub. The intended sense is the genus, and for this reason it is described with the plural, which is the words of the Exalted: ﴿beautiful﴾, the two readings being taken according to meaning. It has been said that it is a collective noun, or a plural whose singular is *'abqariyyah*. Most have explained it as the finest rugs (*'ataq al-zaraby*). From Abu 'Ubayda: it is that which is entirely embroidered carpeting. 

One or more transmitted from Mujahid that it is thick brocade, and from al-Hasan that they are carpets with images in them. You have heard what was transmitted from him concerning *rafraf*, so do not overlook what the conjunction requires.

Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and Nasr ibn Asim al-Jahdari, and Malik ibn Dinar, and Ibn Muhaysin
*(page 125)*
and Zuhayr al-Furqubi, and others, read *rafarif* as a plural that does not take nunation (*la yanşarif*); ﴿green﴾ with the *dad* sukun; ﴿'abqariyy﴾ with the *qaf* kasra and the *ya'* with a shadda. From them also (is the reading) with a *dammah* on the *dad*, and from them also a *fathah* on the *qaf*, as stated by the author of *al-Lawami'*. Then he said: As for the prohibition of nunation for *'abqariyy*, it is because of its juxtaposition with *rafarif*, meaning for the sake of harmony (*mushakalah*); otherwise there is no basis for prohibiting nunation together with the two *ya'*s of the relative, except in poetic necessity. End.

Ibn Khalawayh said: The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, read ﴿on rafarif khudr wa-'abqariyy﴾, and al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin. And it has been transmitted from those we have mentioned ﴿on rafarif khudr wa-'abqariyy﴾ with nunation, and likewise it is transmitted from Malik ibn Dinar. Abu Muhammad al-Marwazi, who was a grammarian, read ﴿on rafarif khidar﴾ on the pattern *fi'al*. The author of *al-Kamil* said: Ibn Musarrif, Ibn Muqsim and Ibn Muhaysin read *rafarif* in the plural. Shibl, Abu Haywa, al-Jahdari and al-Za'farani chose it, and it is the preferred reading because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿khudr﴾. And *'abqariyy* in the plural and with a kasra on the *qaf* without nunation is read by Ibn Muqsim and Ibn Muhaysin, and nunation is transmitted from both of them.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Zuhayr al-Qurqubi read *rafarif* in the plural and without nunation, and Abu Tu'mah al-Madani and Asim, as transmitted from him, read *rafarif* with nunation, and Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, likewise, and *'abqariyy* in the plural with nunation. And from him (is the reading) *'abqariyy* with a *fathah* on the *qaf* and the *ya'*, on the basis that the name of the place is *'abqar* with a *fathah* on the *qaf*, whereas the correct form is *'abqar*. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is read *'abqari* like *madaini*.

Abu Hatim transmitted *'abqariyy* with a *fathah* on the *qaf* and without nunation, and there is no basis for its soundness. Al-Zajjaj said: This reading has no way of being justified, because what exceeds three letters is not pluralized with the *ya'* of the relative; if you pluralized *'abqariyy* you would say *'abaqirah*, like *muhlabiyy* and *mahalibah*, and you do not say *mahalabiyy*.

Ibn Jinni said: As for leaving out the nunation of *'abqariyy*, it is anomalous by analogy, and its anomaly is not to be condemned given that it is in use. Ibn Hisham said: That it is a relative from the plural, like *madā'iniyy*, is false, for whoever reads it this way reads *rafarif khudr* with the intention of harmony (*mujanasah*). If it were as he mentioned it would be singular, and the prohibition of its nunation would not be valid, like *mudā'iniyy*. The transmission of its prohibition of nunation from the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is sound, so it belongs to the category of *kursiyy* and *karasiyy*, and it is of the form of the final plural pattern (*muntaha al-juyu'*), but it deviates from analogy in the addition of letters after the *alif* beyond what is known, as mentioned by al-Suhayli. The author of *al-Kashf* said: The *fathah* on the *qaf* has no justification in any way, and what is mentioned in *al-Muntaqa* from the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is the kasra.

As for the prohibition of nunation, it is not definitively required to be rejected; rather its basis is that it is in the accusative on the locus (*mahall*) of *rafraf*, after the manner of: "They go in Najd and in the lowland (*ghawran*)."

Its being in apposition to ﴿beautiful﴾ is like the apposition of *hur* to *'in* in the reading of Ikrima; as if it were said: "'abqariyy cushions, or beautiful cushions," so it belongs to the category of "garments of character," because one of the two descriptions stands in place of the described thing. Perhaps *'abqar* and *'abaqir* are like *'arafah* and *'arafat*. End. So encompass the aspects of the discussion and do not neglect them.

Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿khudur﴾ with a *dammah* on the *dad*, and this is a rare dialect. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

*O singing-girls in our gathering, strip off from them the reddish and the white.*

And the saying of another:

*I have not belonged to a delicate woman, nor to a coward, nor to a base man on the day of terror, a fleeing one.*

So *shuqr* is the plural of *ashqar* (reddish), and *kashf* is the plural of *akhshaf*, meaning one who flees in war. This is the description by the words of the Exalted: ﴿reclining on rafraf﴾, and so on, rather than the description by His words, glorified is He: ﴿reclining on furush whose linings are of istabraq﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], according to the one who holds that the two earlier gardens are more excellent, because in this description there is an indication that the outer parts (*zahha'ir*) are among what description cannot encompass. And whoever holds that the last two are more excellent says: *rafraf* is what is spread over the back of the one lying on the bed, and the *furush* upon which the *rafraf* is laid are not mentioned; so it is possible that leaving out their mention is for the sake of indicating that description does not encompass them, outer and inner, and this is more eloquent than the first. It is not accepted that those *furush* are the *'abqariyy*. Or one says: *rafraf* means raised bedding, and he left aside any mention of its colour other than green, which is the colour toward which natural dispositions incline most, and which comprises the basic three colours, as the Imam explained, pointing out that these are among what expressions scarcely encompass the reality of. This may be said otherwise too, so reflect.

On the view that the last two are more excellent, and that they belong to a group other than the group indicated by "whoever fears," it should be that the one who fears is one with intense fear, so that it is specific to the most excellent and noblest of believers. Or it may be said: the two (last gardens) together with the first two belong to "whoever fears the station of his Lord," and the meaning is ﴿and for whoever fears the station of his Lord﴾ also: ﴿two gardens﴾, whose description is such-and-such, apart from those two gardens. Upon this it has been said: ﴿two gardens﴾ is a conjunction with the previous ﴿two gardens﴾, and ﴿and beside them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). Some have gone to the view that these two gardens, whether they are more excellent than the first two or not, belong to whoever fears the station of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic; so for him on the Day of Resurrection there are four gardens.

Al-Tabarsi said: The last two are beneath the first two, that is, closer to his palace and his assemblies, so that his joy is doubled by moving from one garden to another, according to what is known of human nature in desiring such, and this is further from the boredom to which humans are subject. You know that the verse admits this with apparent possibility, but what preceded from the hadith of Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with him, rejects it. So if it is sound, even as a *mawquf* (a report ending with a Companion), since the ruling on such is the ruling of a *marfu'* (a report traced to the Prophet), we have no way to turn away from what it requires. It has also been transmitted from him a *marfu'* hadith which al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, indicating that the four gardens are the gardens of Firdaws.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others transmitted from him that he said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The gardens of Firdaws are four: two gardens of gold, its ornaments and its vessels and what is in them; and two gardens of silver, its ornaments and its vessels and what is in them; and nothing stands between the people and looking at their Lord except the mantle of greatness over His face, in the Garden of Eden." The apparent meaning of this is that thousands share in one garden of these gardens. The meaning of His words, "and for whoever fears," and so on, upon this is not hidden.

Then, the ones with restrained gaze (*qasirat al-tarf*) were of mankind, so they are more honoured in rank and more beautiful in appearance than the *hur* who are secluded in pavilions, on the basis that they are the women created in Paradise.

For there has come in the hadith of Umm Salamah: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, are the women of the world better, or the *hur al-'in*? He said: The women of the world are better than the *hur al-'in*, as the excellence of the outer garment over the lining. I said: O Messenger of Allah, and why is that? He said: By their prayer, their fasting and their worship. Allah clothes their faces with light and their bodies with silk, white of face, green of garments, yellow of ornaments, their censers are pearls and their combs are gold. They say: 'Are we not the eternal ones, so we never die? Are we not the ones of delight, so we never despair? Blessed is he for whom we are, and who is for us.'" And there are other reports. This supports the view that the first two gardens are more excellent than the last two. Perhaps He, glorified is He, mentioned reclining first before mentioning the women, because He, mighty and majestic, mentioned fear at the beginning of the verse, when He said, glorified is He: ﴿and for whoever fears the station of his Lord, two gardens﴾. So it was appropriate to hasten to mention what indicates its removal, clearly indicating it, and that is reclining, for it is a characteristic of the secure. And He, glorified is He, delayed its mention a second time after mentioning them, because there was nothing requiring its advancement, and because reclining is something a man ordinarily does after his mind is free of what the house needs of food, drink and a singing-girl who is in it. And if we say that the *hur* are like the maidservants in the house, then the matter of advancing and delaying would be more fitting.

The Imam said on this: The people of Paradise have no weariness or movement; they are constantly in delight. But people in this world are of kinds: some gather with their wives in a hurried gathering, and when they have fulfilled their need they wash and disperse on the earth to earn; and some are hesitant in seeking earnings, and when they obtain them they return to their families and rest from whatever weariness has befallen them, either before fulfilling their desire or after it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, said of the people of Paradise: "reclining," it is said that their gathering with their families is reclining after the gathering, so that it is known that they are constantly in stillness. It is not hidden that this, for all that is in it, does not settle the question, for someone may say: why was the order of advancing and delaying not reversed in the two places, although it also includes an indication of that? Then he mentioned a second aspect concerning that, which, for all that is in it, is built upon what has no basis in the reports, so reflect.

It has been said: what hangs down from the bedsteads of fine garments. Al-Raghib said: a kind of garment likened to gardens. Ibn Jarir and a group transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: *al-rafraf* are the gardens of Paradise. And he transmitted from Abd ibn Humayd something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is, as in *al-Bahr*, from *raff al-nabt*, meaning plants that flourish and are beautiful. It is also said that *rafraf* is any wide garment, and the thin silk brocade garments, and the edges of a tent or pavilion that rest on the ground, below the guy-ropes and pegs. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that this meaning has been said here, but in it there is something (to consider).

﴿And of 'abqari﴾: it is a relative adjective (*mansub*) to *'Abqar*, which the Arabs claim is the name of the land of the jinn, so they attribute to it every wondrous and rare thing among carpets and other things. Its meaning is therefore "the marvelous, rare thing." From this is what came concerning Umar al-Faruq, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen an *'abqari* who fabricates a fabrication (*fariyah*)." Because that relative sense has been forgotten, it has been said that it is not a relative adjective but is like *kursi* and *bukhti*, as transmitted from Qutrub. The intended sense is the genus, and for this reason it is described with the plural, which is the words of the Exalted: ﴿beautiful﴾, the two readings being taken according to meaning. It has been said that it is a collective noun, or a plural whose singular is *'abqariyyah*. Most have explained it as the finest rugs (*'ataq al-zaraby*). From Abu 'Ubayda: it is that which is entirely embroidered carpeting. 

One or more transmitted from Mujahid that it is thick brocade, and from al-Hasan that they are carpets with images in them. You have heard what was transmitted from him concerning *rafraf*, so do not overlook what the conjunction requires.

Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and Nasr ibn Asim al-Jahdari, and Malik ibn Dinar, and Ibn Muhaysin
*(page 125)*
and Zuhayr al-Furqubi, and others, read *rafarif* as a plural that does not take nunation (*la yanşarif*); ﴿green﴾ with the *dad* sukun; ﴿'abqariyy﴾ with the *qaf* kasra and the *ya'* with a shadda. From them also (is the reading) with a *dammah* on the *dad*, and from them also a *fathah* on the *qaf*, as stated by the author of *al-Lawami'*. Then he said: As for the prohibition of nunation for *'abqariyy*, it is because of its juxtaposition with *rafarif*, meaning for the sake of harmony (*mushakalah*); otherwise there is no basis for prohibiting nunation together with the two *ya'*s of the relative, except in poetic necessity. End.

Ibn Khalawayh said: The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, read ﴿on rafarif khudr wa-'abqariyy﴾, and al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin. And it has been transmitted from those we have mentioned ﴿on rafarif khudr wa-'abqariyy﴾ with nunation, and likewise it is transmitted from Malik ibn Dinar. Abu Muhammad al-Marwazi, who was a grammarian, read ﴿on rafarif khidar﴾ on the pattern *fi'al*. The author of *al-Kamil* said: Ibn Musarrif, Ibn Muqsim and Ibn Muhaysin read *rafarif* in the plural. Shibl, Abu Haywa, al-Jahdari and al-Za'farani chose it, and it is the preferred reading because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿khudr﴾. And *'abqariyy* in the plural and with a kasra on the *qaf* without nunation is read by Ibn Muqsim and Ibn Muhaysin, and nunation is transmitted from both of them.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Zuhayr al-Qurqubi read *rafarif* in the plural and without nunation, and Abu Tu'mah al-Madani and Asim, as transmitted from him, read *rafarif* with nunation, and Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, likewise, and *'abqariyy* in the plural with nunation. And from him (is the reading) *'abqariyy* with a *fathah* on the *qaf* and the *ya'*, on the basis that the name of the place is *'abqar* with a *fathah* on the *qaf*, whereas the correct form is *'abqar*. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is read *'abqari* like *madaini*.

Abu Hatim transmitted *'abqariyy* with a *fathah* on the *qaf* and without nunation, and there is no basis for its soundness. Al-Zajjaj said: This reading has no way of being justified, because what exceeds three letters is not pluralized with the *ya'* of the relative; if you pluralized *'abqariyy* you would say *'abaqirah*, like *muhlabiyy* and *mahalibah*, and you do not say *mahalabiyy*.

Ibn Jinni said: As for leaving out the nunation of *'abqariyy*, it is anomalous by analogy, and its anomaly is not to be condemned given that it is in use. Ibn Hisham said: That it is a relative from the plural, like *madā'iniyy*, is false, for whoever reads it this way reads *rafarif khudr* with the intention of harmony (*mujanasah*). If it were as he mentioned it would be singular, and the prohibition of its nunation would not be valid, like *mudā'iniyy*. The transmission of its prohibition of nunation from the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is sound, so it belongs to the category of *kursiyy* and *karasiyy*, and it is of the form of the final plural pattern (*muntaha al-juyu'*), but it deviates from analogy in the addition of letters after the *alif* beyond what is known, as mentioned by al-Suhayli. Perhaps *'abqar* and *'abaqir* are like *'arafah* and *'arafat*. End. So encompass the aspects of the discussion and do not neglect them.

Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿khudur﴾ with a *dammah* on the *dad*, and this is a rare dialect. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

*O singing-girls in our gathering, strip off from them the reddish and the white.*

And the saying of another:

*I have not belonged to a delicate woman, nor to a coward, nor to a base man on the day of terror, a fleeing one.*

So *shuqr* is the plural of *ashqar* (reddish), and *kashf* is the plural of *akhshaf*, meaning one who flees in war. This is the description by the words of the Exalted: ﴿reclining on rafraf﴾, and so on, rather than the description by His words, glorified is He: ﴿reclining on furush whose linings are of istabraq﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], according to the one who holds that the two earlier gardens are more excellent, because in this description there is an indication that the outer parts (*zahha'ir*) are among what description cannot encompass. And whoever holds that the last two are more excellent says: *rafraf* is what is spread over the back of the one lying on the bed, and the *furush* upon which the *rafraf* is laid are not mentioned; so it is possible that leaving out their mention is for the sake of indicating that description does not encompass them, outer and inner, and this is more eloquent than the first. It is not accepted that those *furush* are the *'abqariyy*. Or one says: *rafraf* means raised bedding, and he left aside any mention of its colour other than green, which is the colour toward which natural dispositions incline most, and which comprises the basic three colours, as the Imam explained, pointing out that these are among what expressions scarcely encompass the reality of. This may be said otherwise too, so reflect.

On the view that the last two are more excellent, and that they belong to a group other than the group indicated by "whoever fears," it should be that the one who fears is one with intense fear, so that it is specific to the most excellent and noblest of believers. Or it may be said: the two (last gardens) together with the first two belong to "whoever fears the station of his Lord," and the meaning is ﴿and for whoever fears the station of his Lord﴾ also: ﴿two gardens﴾, whose description is such-and-such, apart from those two gardens. Upon this it has been said: ﴿two gardens﴾ is a conjunction with the previous ﴿two gardens﴾, and ﴿and beside them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). Some have gone to the view that these two gardens, whether they are more excellent than the first two or not, belong to whoever fears the station of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic; so for him on the Day of Resurrection there are four gardens.

Al-Tabarsi said: The last two are beneath the first two, that is, closer to his palace and his assemblies, so that his joy is doubled by moving from one garden to another, according to what is known of human nature in desiring such, and this is further from the boredom to which humans are subject. You know that the verse admits this with apparent possibility, but what preceded from the hadith of Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with him, rejects it. So if it is sound, even as a *mawquf* (a report ending with a Companion), since the ruling on such is the ruling of a *marfu'* (a report traced to the Prophet), we have no way to turn away from what it requires. It has also been transmitted from him a *marfu'* hadith which al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, indicating that the four gardens are the gardens of Firdaws.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others transmitted from him that he said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The gardens of Firdaws are four: two gardens of gold, its ornaments and its vessels and what is in them; and two gardens of silver, its ornaments and its vessels and what is in them; and nothing stands between the people and looking at their Lord except the mantle of greatness over His face, in the Garden of Eden." The apparent meaning of this is that thousands share in one garden of these gardens. The meaning of His words, "and for whoever fears," and so on, upon this is not hidden.

Then, the ones with restrained gaze (*qasirat al-tarf*) were of mankind, so they are more honoured in rank and more beautiful in appearance than the *hur* who are secluded in pavilions, on the basis that they are the women created in Paradise.

For there has come in the hadith of Umm Salamah: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, are the women of the world better, or the *hur al-'in*? He said: The women of the world are better than the *hur al-'in*, as the excellence of the outer garment over the lining. I said: O Messenger of Allah, and why is that? He said: By their prayer, their fasting and their worship. Allah clothes their faces with light and their bodies with silk, white of face, green of garments, yellow of ornaments, their censers are pearls and their combs are gold. They say: 'Are we not the eternal ones, so we never die? Are we not the ones of delight, so we never despair? Blessed is he for whom we are, and who is for us.'" And there are other reports. This supports the view that the first two gardens are more excellent than the last two. Perhaps He, glorified is He, mentioned reclining first before mentioning the women, because He, mighty and majestic, mentioned fear at the beginning of the verse, when He said, glorified is He: ﴿and for whoever fears the station of his Lord, two gardens﴾. So it was appropriate to hasten to mention what indicates its removal, clearly indicating it, and that is reclining, for it is a characteristic of the secure. And He, glorified is He, delayed its mention a second time after mentioning them, because there was nothing requiring its advancement, and because reclining is something a man ordinarily does after his mind is free of what the house needs of food, drink and a singing-girl who is in it. And if we say that the *hur* are like the maidservants in the house, then the matter of advancing and delaying would be more fitting.

The Imam said on this: The people of Paradise have no weariness or movement; they are constantly in delight. But people in this world are of kinds: some gather with their wives in a hurried gathering, and when they have fulfilled their need they wash and disperse on the earth to earn; and some are hesitant in seeking earnings, and when they obtain them they return to their families and rest from whatever weariness has befallen them, either before fulfilling their desire or after it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, said of the people of Paradise: "reclining," it is said that their gathering with their families is reclining after the gathering, so that it is known that they are constantly in stillness. It is not hidden that this, for all that is in it, does not settle the question, for someone may say: why was the order of advancing and delaying not reversed in the two places, although it also includes an indication of that? Then he mentioned a second aspect concerning that, which, for all that is in it, is built upon what has no basis in the reports, so reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 55, verses 77–78:**

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ is a declaration of His exaltation and sanctification, Exalted is He, in which is an affirmation of what was mentioned in this noble surah of His favours, Majestic is His station, which overflow upon the days. So ﴿tabaraka﴾ (blessed) is in the sense of ﴿ta'ala﴾ (exalted), because it carries its meaning, and it is more fitting to the attribute that follows. It has been related in the hadiths: "Exalted is His name" (ta'ala ismuhu), meaning: exalted is His glorious name, of which is that with which the surah begins, the name ﴿al-Rahman﴾ (the Most Merciful), which announces the outpouring of detailed favours, and He is高 above what does not befit His dignity, among the matters of which is the denial of His bounties and rejecting them. And if the state of His name, by its connection to its indication of Him, Glorified is He, is thus, then what do you think of His Most Holy and Most High Essence??

It has been said: the "name" (ism) here means "attribute" (sifa), because it is a sign of what it describes. It has been said: it is superfluous (muqhamun), as in the saying of one who said: "Then the name of peace be upon you both." It has been said: it means "the named" (musamma). Some have claimed that what is most fitting to the purpose of this noble surah, which is the multiplicity of favours and blessings, is to interpret ﴿tabaraka﴾ as "its goods have multiplied" (kathurat khayratuhu). Then there is no distance in attributing this meaning to His name, Exalted is He, since by it rain is sought so that one is given rain, and by it help is sought so that one is aided. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ is an attribute of the Lord, and describing Him, Majestic and Exalted, with this is a completion of what was mentioned of exaltation and affirmation. Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read ﴿dhu﴾ (Possessor) with a nominative ending (raf'), on the basis that it is an attribute of the Name. Its description with "majesty and honour" in the sense of "bestowing honour" is clear.

* * *

This is "from the door of allusion" (min bab al-ishara). In some verses, ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ is an allusion to what He, Glorified is He, deposited in the pure holy souls of the knowledge of divine truths in summary form, when He, Mighty and Majestic, settled upon the throne of mercifulness. ﴿He created man﴾, the complete, all-encompassing one, ﴿taught him the expression﴾, which is the detailing of those summary sciences. ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation﴾ [al-Qiyama: 18, 19]. ﴿The sun and the moon [move] by calculation﴾ points to the sun of prophethood and the moon of walaya (sainthood), which revolve in the orbit of human existence according to the reckoning of manifestations and the degrees of readiness. ﴿And the star﴾ refers to the lower powers, ﴿and the tree﴾ to the higher readinesses, ﴿prostrate﴾, humbling themselves before Him, Exalted is He, upon returning to Him, Glorified is He. ﴿And the heaven﴾, the heaven of the holy divine powers, ﴿He raised it﴾ above the earth of humanity. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾, the distinguishing faculty. ﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾: do not exceed, when taking lower portions and giving higher rights.

It is permissible that ﴿al-mizan﴾ (the balance) means the pure Sharia, for it is a balance by which the perfect is distinguished from the deficient. ﴿And the earth﴾, the earth of humanity, ﴿He set it﴾, spread it out and laid it as a bed ﴿for the creatures﴾, for the human powers. ﴿In it is fruit﴾ of fruits whose attributes of action are known. ﴿And the palm tree, having sheaths﴾, which is the human tree, the greatest manifestation, having stages each stage covered by another stage. ﴿And the grain﴾ is the grain of love sown in the fields of hearts free from weeds. ﴿With its husk﴾ are the leaves of unveilings. ﴿And the fragrant plant﴾ is the fragrance of witnessing. ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾: the Lord of the east of the sun of prophethood and the east of the moon of walaya in the corporeal world, and the Lord of their two wests in the spiritual world. ﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting together﴾: the sea of the heaven of higher powers and the sea of the earth of lower powers. ﴿Between them is a barrier﴾, the heart's barrier, ﴿from which emerge pearls and coral﴾: kinds of lights of secrets and fires of longings. ﴿And His are the ships, raised high﴾: the ships of thoughts subjected in the sea of man. ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾: whoever has not smelled the scent of existence. ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾: the aspect that faces Him, Glorified is He, and these are His affairs, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Possessor of Majesty﴾, that is, complete independence from all manifestations, ﴿and Honour﴾: the general overflow that pours onto recipients according to what they are prepared for and ask for by the tongue of their state. To this refers His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾, etc. (page 128).

The Greatest Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, cited His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Every day He is in some matter﴾ as evidence for the excellence of change (al-talawwun), and likewise he cited it as evidence for the non-permanence of the substance moment by moment. In this same vein is what has been said about the verses that follow. Some scholars have mentioned that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ has been mentioned thirty-one times: eight of them after enumerating the wonders of His creation and mentioning the beginning and the return; seven after mentioning what suggests the Fire and its terrors, corresponding to the number of the gates of Hell; and eight in describing the first two gardens, and the same number in describing the two gardens below them, corresponding to the number of the gates of Paradise. It seems that this points to the fact that whoever believes the first eight and acts in accordance with them deserves both gardens from God, Exalted is He, and He will shield him from Hell, which has seven gates. And God, Exalted is He, knows best the allusions of His Book, the realities of His address, and the subtleties of His speech, which minds cannot encompass. ﴿And blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾
